primary_cause: Anticipation COVID would sharply reduce elective robotic surgeries. No clearly dated company-specific announcement Mar 17-20. Later disclosed COVID-driven deferral had significant negative impact and withdrew 2020 guidance. CA issued statewide stay-at-home Mar 19
secondary_factors: Broad risk-off trading into one of worst weeks of 2020 crash
store_description: The stock 3.4% decline looks mostly tied to the market beginning to discount a severe procedure-volume hit not to a fresh March 20 press release. Intuitive later confirmed exactly that pattern saying deferred elective procedures would materially hurt results.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Mar 20 Treasury/IRS extended federal filing deadline to Jul 15 from Apr 15. Directly affected Intuit seasonal TurboTax revenue timing. Later said COVID and filing-delay extension lowered fiscal Q3 results
secondary_factors: COVID pressure on small-business customers which Intuit later said began in mid-March
store_description: This is one of the cleaner names. The March 20 deadline shift pushed the core tax-season monetization window out by three months and Intuit later explicitly said both the IRS extension and weakening small-business trends hurt revenue operating income and EPS versus prior guidance.

primary_cause: No fresh Honeywell-specific filing or guidance cut Mar 17-20. Reuters reported coronavirus crisis rocking airlines and planemakers. Aerospace exposure amid airline and planemaker collapse
secondary_factors: Broad industrial recession fears. General market liquidation. CA Mar 19 stay-at-home order
store_description: Honeywell drop appears mainly tied to its cyclical aerospace and industrial exposure rather than a company-specific announcement. With airlines slashing schedules and aerospace manufacturing coming under acute pressure investors were repricing HON for a deep multi-segment demand shock.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Home Depot announced Mar 18 stores would temporarily close daily at 6pm and extending paid time off. CA Mar 19 stay-at-home order. COVID operating disruption and uncertainty around store traffic and labor costs
secondary_factors: Broad consumer and retail liquidation despite essential-retailer status
store_description: Unlike later in the pandemic March 20 was still the stage where investors were treating almost all brick-and-mortar retail as operationally impaired. Home Depot reduced hours signaled immediate disruption and new shutdown orders made near-term comps staffing and project demand hard to forecast.

primary_cause: No fresh Goldman-specific corporate announcement Mar 17-20. Goldman publishing increasingly severe macro forecasts. Financial-sector selloff on recession credit and funding-stress fears
secondary_factors: Goldman own grim macro outlook. Generalized deleveraging in banks and brokers
store_description: This looks less like issuer news and more like a brutal sector repricing. Investors were discounting collapsing deal activity weaker asset prices funding stress and future credit losses across the banking system and GS fell harder than the index.

primary_cause: Expected advertising slowdown as COVID hit brand spending. Google promised nationwide coronavirus info portal was delayed. Later Reuters showed YouTube brand advertising declined in mid-March
secondary_factors: Product-execution embarrassment around delayed COVID portal. Broader tech selloff
store_description: The key fundamental issue was ad exposure not search usage. As the economy shut down brand advertisers pulled back sharply and Reuters later reported Alphabet specifically saw YouTube brand advertising weaken in mid-March.

primary_cause: No clearly dated IBM-specific release Mar 17-20. Concern global lockdowns would hurt enterprise spending consulting and large IT projects. IBM integrating Red Hat and carrying elevated debt
secondary_factors: Balance-sheet concerns after Red Hat deal. Marketwide liquidation
store_description: There does not appear to have been a fresh IBM-specific bombshell in the prior three days. The stock likely traded down on the view that recession and lockdowns would delay customer projects and pressure legacy services demand.

primary_cause: No negative Gilead-specific Reuters item Mar 17-20. Remdesivir increasingly viewed as potential COVID treatment. No clear fresh negative — likely reversal and profit-taking after prior remdesivir strength plus market stress
secondary_factors: Healthcare sold off too on March 20 despite defensive status
store_description: This is not a case where a crisp bad-news catalyst was found. The better interpretation is that GILD after being treated as a COVID-treatment beneficiary still got caught in a sharp liquidation day and likely saw some unwinding of earlier defensive and therapeutic positioning.

primary_cause: No fresh General Dynamics-specific Mar 17-20 release. Defense and business-jet sentiment deteriorated. Reuters and Defense News documented growing concern about defense-industrial-base disruption. Defense and business-jet demand and supply-chain worries
secondary_factors: Broad industrial selloff
store_description: GD decline looks more like a sector repricing than a stock-specific event. The market was beginning to price operational disruptions across the defense supply chain and severe weakness in business aviation both relevant to General Dynamics.

primary_cause: No fresh Emerson-specific announcement Mar 17-20. Meaningful exposure to industrial capex and energy markets under severe pressure. Industrial and energy end-market recession fears
secondary_factors: General market liquidation
store_description: This looks like a cyclical industrial repricing rather than a discrete company event. By March 20 investors were assuming a deep freeze in capital spending across manufacturing and energy which directly threatened Emerson automation and industrial businesses.

primary_cause: No fresh Duke-specific corporate announcement Mar 17-20. Utilities sold off sharply despite defensive label. CA stay-at-home order underscored scope of economic stop. Violent utility-sector selloff tied to recession and forced deleveraging
secondary_factors: Fear of weaker commercial and industrial load. Liquidity-driven selling
store_description: DUK near-9% drop is too large for normal utility trading and looks primarily macro and sector-driven. The market was no longer treating utilities as a clean safe haven because the shutdown threatened electricity demand from businesses while leveraged investors were selling almost anything liquid.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC context. Reuters Mar 12 reported Disney would close parks in CA and FL and Disneyland Paris through month-end. By Mar 20 investors absorbing broader implications for cruises theatrical releases and ESPN and live sports
secondary_factors: Movie-release delays. Suspended cruises. Sports shutdown hurting ESPN. Parks closures alone jeopardized segment that generated $21.6B in 2019 revenue
store_description: Disney had one of the clearest COVID earnings hits in the entire market. Parks closures alone jeopardized a segment that generated $21.6B in 2019 revenue and the simultaneous shutdown in sports and theaters meant investors were suddenly repricing multiple Disney profit engines at once.

primary_cause: Same setup as GOOGL. Delayed COVID-information portal. Growing expectation of advertising slowdown. Expected ad-market deterioration
secondary_factors: No separate Class C-specific catalyst. Investors discounting weaker ad demand particularly in brand advertising
store_description: There was no separate GOOG-specific catalyst. GOOG and GOOGL were reacting to the same Alphabet fundamentals. Investors were discounting weaker ad demand particularly in brand advertising which Reuters later confirmed had deteriorated in mid-March.

primary_cause: No Cisco earnings or guidance change Mar 17-20. Reuters coverage focused on work-from-home surge creating cybersecurity issues. Anticipated slowdown in enterprise capex and hardware orders
secondary_factors: Work-from-home security and disruption headlines. Broad tech selloff. More network usage but sharply weaker corporate spending intent
store_description: Cisco was caught between two opposing forces: more network usage but sharply weaker corporate spending intent. On balance the market appears to have priced the recessionary capex hit more heavily which better explains a 5.6% decline during this phase of the crash.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Reuters reported Nike would close all stores across U.S. Canada Western Europe Australia New Zealand by Mar 27. Already said Mar 15 closing stores. COVID store closures and implied hit to near-term retail sales
secondary_factors: Broader consumer discretionary stress. Supply-chain uncertainty. Widespread retailer shutdowns globally
store_description: Nike March 23 drop lines up well with the realization that a substantial part of its physical retail footprint across key developed markets would be closed. Investors were forced to model a sharp near-term sales hit even though China had shown some signs of reopening.

primary_cause: No fresh NextEra-specific company catalyst Mar 20-23. Mar 23 was market bottom day. Utility-sector weakness despite Fed intervention. Recession-driven demand fears still dominating
secondary_factors: Interest-rate and credit stress. Indiscriminate selling near market bottom
store_description: This looks primarily macro and sectoral not issuer-specific. The Fed March 23 announcement stabilized credit broadly but utilities were still under pressure as investors weighed weaker commercial load capital-intensity and continued forced selling into the trough of the crisis.

primary_cause: No fresh Merck-specific negative Mar 20-23. Not yet leading COVID winner in market narrative. Defensive healthcare names still sold off sharply around Mar 23 bottom
secondary_factors: Rotation away from some defensives amid extreme volatility and cash raising
store_description: MRK 7% decline seems more about market structure than stock news. Even high-quality pharma names were being sold into the March panic as portfolios de-risked and investors preferred liquidity over defensiveness.

primary_cause: No fresh Altria-specific Mar 20-23 press release. Already-known damage from Juul investment including $4.1B impairment disclosed late January. Broad consumer-defensive selloff plus ongoing skepticism tied to Juul and regulatory overhang
secondary_factors: Marketwide deleveraging. Recession fears
store_description: No strong evidence of a new Altria event inside the exact three-day window. The best read is that MO was hit by the same indiscriminate selling that hit much of the market near the March 23 bottom with the already-damaged Juul thesis leaving the stock less able to act as a defensive haven.

primary_cause: Market concern broader elective-procedure and medical-device demand would weaken despite ventilator upside. Medtronic announced Mar 18-19 would more than double ventilator manufacturing capacity
secondary_factors: Supply-chain complexity and execution risk around surge production. Ventilator headlines not enough to offset broader concern
store_description: The ventilator headlines were not enough to offset the market broader concern that hospitals would defer non-urgent procedures hurting the rest of Medtronic portfolio. So even with demand surging in one product line investors seem to have focused on the wider medtech slowdown.

primary_cause: Reuters late January reported Mondelez expected coronavirus to hurt Q1 sales. Mar 23 Mondelez announced $15M global commitment (philanthropic). Ongoing concern about COVID-related sales and supply-chain disruption
secondary_factors: Consumer staples not fully immune to liquidation at March bottom
store_description: The March 23 drop was likely less about the same-day charitable announcement and more about investors continuing to price the operational drag Mondelez had already flagged from the outbreak. MDLZ looks like a mild continuation move on existing COVID disruption concerns plus broad market stress.
